bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

itinerary: Commonly done car-to-car in a single long day (about 7.5-8.75 hours round trip reported from Merritt Lake TH for Howard alone or Howard+Mastiff combined). A 2-day version is also used, especially for spring snow climbs or when combining multiple Nason Ridge summits: Day 1 — trailhead to a bivy near Crescent Lake or the summit (about 12 miles, 6,000-6,400 ft gain); Day 2 — summit (if not reached Day 1) and return to the trailhead.

name: North Face (North Peak)
approach: Lake Serene Trail (#1068) from the Mount Index Road trailhead, 3.6 miles / roughly 1,920 ft gain to Lake Serene (about 1.5-2 hours), then talus and grass slopes on the west side of the lake (near an old rockslide) to reach the base of the North Peak's broken, bushy lower spur.
descent: Descend via the North Face route's approach line/rib back toward Lake Serene.
itinerary: Common plan: Day 1 — hike in to Lake Serene (or bivy at the lake/talus basin below the route); Day 2 — pre-dawn start, climb the North Face (roughly a full day with the approach), and descend/rappel back to the lake, hiking out that evening. Strong parties occasionally do it car-to-car in one very long day.

name: South Slope - South Face (Standard Route)
approach: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead (~2,500 ft, via SR-20 and Lost River Road/Forest Road 5400 west of Winthrop), follow the Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail over Robinson Pass and down into the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage. Continue north down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction and, about 4.8 miles beyond the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail up Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp and water source below Lago's west side. From Fred's Lake, follow the unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail (or cross-country) east across the upper Eureka Creek basin - the creek crossing can be difficult when swollen with snowmelt - to reach Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge. The shortest road-based approach is roughly 16 miles one-way, typically covered over 1-2 days.
descent: Reverse the South Slope, or descend via the adjacent Southwest Slope talus back to Shellrock Basin.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

itinerary: A common 3-day plan: Day 1 - hike in from the Robinson Creek or Slate Pass trailhead to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin. Day 2 - climb Mount Lago (often combined with Mount Carru via the connecting saddle) from a Shellrock Basin camp, roughly a half-day round trip. Day 3 - hike out. Many parties extend to 4-5 days to add Osceola Peak, Mount Rolo, or a full Pasayten ridge traverse (e.g. via Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain).

waypoints.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass

name: Entiat Ice Fall
approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the North Face: Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft) via FR 6211, up the Phelps Creek Trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the climber's trail into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,100-6,200 ft, ~5 miles). From camp, continue toward the Seven Fingered Jack-Maude col/Ice Lakes area and descend to the Entiat Glacier to reach the icefall.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

bivy.name: Leroy Basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
bivy.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

itinerary: Day 1: Approach ~4,000 ft of gain over several hours from the trailhead to a bivy site above Ice Lakes. Day 2: Descend to and cross the Entiat Glacier, climb the icefall (running belay through ice steps) then ~900 ft of 4th/low-5th class rock to the summit, descend the South Ridge back toward camp. Day 3: Hike out.

name: Nothing Couloir
approach: Same lower approach as the North Face/Entiat Icefall routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft) via FR 6211, up the Phelps Creek Trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the climber's trail into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,100-6,200 ft, ~5 miles), continuing onto the peak's west side to reach the base of the couloir system near the standard West/South Slopes route.
descent: South Shoulder, making a loop back toward Leroy Creek Basin.

bivy.name: Leroy Basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.
bivy.water: Reliable — clear streams through the basin, though upper snowfields are what feed them and a very late-season camp may need to walk down for water
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful at the trailhead. No campfires this high — carry a stove. Use the existing sites; the basin is small and the meadow ground scars quickly.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites in a flat basin, comfortably a few parties, and the standard climbers' base for this side of the crest

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

itinerary: Day 1: Hike ~5 mi / ~2,700 ft from the Phelps Creek Trailhead to a camp in Leroy Creek Basin. Day 2: Approach the west side of the peak, climb the Nothing Couloir (class 3-4 slabs, ~1,500 ft) to the summit ridge and summit, then descend via the South Shoulder in a loop back to camp. Day 3: Hike out.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: The standard approach is the North Fork Quinault River Trail, about 16 miles one-way to a high camp at Low Divide. The Elwha River Trail from Whiskey Bend also reaches Low Divide, but it is far longer (~28 miles one-way, plus roughly 7 miles each way of hiking or biking, since the Elwha access road has been closed to vehicles beyond Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage) and suits parties traversing from the north. From high camp, travel off-trail over talus and heather toward the Noyes-Meany col and up the standard slopes.
descent: Reverse the route back to camp near Low Divide, then hike out the Elwha or North Fork Quinault trail.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

itinerary: Multi-day backpack with a high camp near Low Divide, reached via the North Fork Quinault River Trail (~16 mi), or the much longer Elwha River Trail from Whiskey Bend (~28 mi, lengthened by the Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, which has closed the road to vehicles beyond Madison Falls since November 2017).

waypoints.name: North Fork Quinault Trailhead (North Shore Road, road's end)
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha

name: Standard Scramble (Jefferson Creek / Hamma Hamma approach)
approach: From Hoodsport, drive about 14 miles north on US 101 to Hamma Hamma River Road (FR 25); follow it roughly 6.5 miles to FR 2480, then FR 2480 about 3 miles to FR 2401, then FR 2401 roughly 7–7.5 miles to the Jefferson Creek crossing / Jefferson Lake Trailhead area (~2,440 ft). A faint boot path on the north side of the creek leads through forest and brush into the basins below Pershing's east side, then up gullies to the summit ridge. Confirm current road status with Olympic National Forest before driving — FR 2480/2401 have a history of washouts and occasional fire closures. From the boot path, the route rises via a rocky gully to a small basin around 4,300 ft, then continues into a basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft before the final snow/rock gully to the ridge.
descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the ridge crest and the short Class 4 step, then descend the snow/rock gully and basins back to the Jefferson Creek trail and trailhead.

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for Mount Pershing and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

itinerary: Long day trip (~8 miles round trip, 10–11 hours) from the Jefferson Creek trailhead off FR 2401 in the Hamma Hamma drainage; a basin camp is an option for a more relaxed overnight pace.

name: West Ridge
approach: From US Highway 2 near Index, turn onto Forest Road 62 (also called No Name Creek Road / Proctor Creek Road / Cavanaugh Lake Road). Follow FR-62 about 3.4-3.5 miles to the first junction (~1,600-1,650 ft) and bear left. Continue about 1 mile to a second junction (~2,380 ft) and bear left again. Drive roughly another 0.7-1 mile of increasingly rough road to its end (~2,800 ft), where there is a small pullout/parking area. An unmarked, steep, well-trodden gully directly opposite the pullout marks the boot-path trailhead. Note: FR-62 crosses private industrial timberland and its gate at the highway is frequently locked at the owner's discretion — some parties have had to walk or e-bike an additional ~5+ miles and ~2,500 ft of road to reach this trailhead.
descent: Descend the same West Ridge boot path back to the FR-62 trailhead.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

itinerary: Single-day, car-to-car outing: drive FR-62 to the road-end trailhead (allow extra time/mileage if the highway gate is locked), climb the West Ridge boot path to the summit (roughly 2-3 hours of climbing), enjoy summit views, then descend the same way. Total car-to-car time is commonly reported as 4.5+ hours given the steepness and route-finding, longer in winter conditions or if the road gate forces an extended approach.

name: East Ridge (Iodine Gulch – Bathtub Lakes)
approach: From the Verlot Public Service Center on the Mountain Loop Highway, continue east about 4.6 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 4020 (Schweitzer Creek Road, signed for Boardman Lake/Ashland Lakes/Bear-Pinnacle Lake). Follow FR 4020 for 2.7 miles to a junction, take the right fork onto FR 4021, and continue 1.4 miles on a rough road to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead (about 2,700 ft; small ~15-car lot, no toilet). Hike the Pinnacle Lake Trail to the lake, walk around its southwest shore to Iodine Creek, and follow the creek up through Iodine Gulch to its top; turn right and continue a short distance to the Bathtub Lakes basin. From there, continue scrambling west to reach Mount Pilchuck's summit. In October the road to Pinnacle Lake trailhead is rough enough that high clearance is advisable; in a high-water year the lake trail itself can wash out.
descent: Reverse the route back through Bathtub Lakes and Iodine Gulch to Pinnacle Lake and the trailhead.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a state conservation area rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the federal pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

itinerary: Single day: drive to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead, hike to Pinnacle Lake, scramble via Iodine Gulch to Bathtub Lakes (optional turnaround point), then continue to the summit and return the same way — a longer, more committing full-day outing than the standard trail.

waypoints.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck

name: Mount Pilchuck Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From Granite Falls, follow WA-92 east and then the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 10-11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile past Verlot, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right (south) onto Mount Pilchuck Road (FR 42). Follow FR 42 for about 6.8 miles — rough, washboarded gravel for the first ~4.7 miles and paved for the last ~1.9, with the gravel's condition varying by year — to the Mount Pilchuck Trailhead parking area (roughly 3,000-3,100 ft). In years when FR 42 is gated below the trailhead (common in shoulder season), the hike instead starts from the Heather Lake Trailhead, adding roughly 5 miles and substantial elevation gain each way.
descent: Descend the same Mount Pilchuck Trail back to the FR 42 trailhead; there is no separate descent route.
itinerary: Single-day round trip: drive to the FR 42 trailhead, hike up via Trail #700, spend time at the lookout, then descend the same trail — a full day out once drive time from the Seattle/Everett area is included.

name: Hester Lake Route
approach: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,400 ft). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail, crossing several creeks, toward the Hester Lake basin (roughly 5-6 miles) before leaving the trail to begin the off-trail scramble.
descent: Descend the same general line back through the boulder field and Hester Lake basin to the Dingford Creek Trail; several parties report their descent line diverging from the ascent for lack of a fixed route.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is cut by a washout at milepost 17.3 that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft; the Forest Service's road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 lists it with no reopening date. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

itinerary: Full, often long day: Dingford Creek TH -> ~5-6 mi trail to the Hester Lake basin -> off-trail gully/boulder-field/ridge scramble to the summit -> reverse descent. At least one trip report logged roughly 10.5 hours car-to-car; start early and carry a headlamp.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Ridge
approach: From Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20, MP 134) hike the Ross Lake shoreline trail ~7 mi to the Big Beaver Trail junction (or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing to shorten this), then continue ~5 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Thirtynine Mile Creek/Camp. Leave the trail there and climb a brushy forested rib to gain the south ridge at a ~6,600 ft saddle. Round trip from the Big Beaver Landing water-taxi drop is roughly 18 miles with 7,000+ ft of elevation gain, typically done over 2-3 days; walking the lakeshore both ways instead adds about 14 miles. From the saddle, follow the ridge crest (Class 1-2) past points 7,361 ft and 7,547 ft to a short Class 3 step below the true summit; Luna Camp, about 5 miles farther up Big Beaver Trail, is the start of the separate Southwest Rib route, not this one.
descent: Reverse the south ridge and the brushy rib back down to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then follow Big Beaver Trail back to Ross Lake.
itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: hike or water-taxi in to the Thirtynine Mile Creek area, high camp at the saddle on the south ridge crest, summit day via the ridge, then exit back down Big Beaver Trail.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Trail junction (via Ross Dam)
Off-trail departure onto Thirtynine Mile Ridge
Saddle camp below Point 6690, South Ridge

name: Southwest Rib
approach: As for the South/Southeast Ridge: SR-20 to the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134), then the Ross Dam Trail and Big Beaver Trail (or the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing) up the Big Beaver Creek valley to Luna Camp, the base camp for this route.
descent: Most parties descend the same Southwest Rib line, or link with the South/Southeast Ridge as a loop (documented in at least one trip report: SE ridge up, SW rib down).

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: hike/boat in to Luna Camp on Day 1, climb the rib to the summit and return to camp on Day 2 (or continue over the South/Southeast Ridge as a loop), hike/boat out on Day 3.

name: Pika Slab
approach: From I-5 exit 208 head east 4 miles on Highway 530 to Arlington, then continue east on SR 530 for 28 miles to Darrington. At the four-way intersection in town turn right onto the Mountain Loop Highway and follow paved then graveled road for roughly 12.5-14 miles to a prominent Mount Pugh sign, where FR 2095 branches off on the left. FR 2095 is narrow, one-lane and unpaved; drive it about 1.5 miles to the signed trailhead on the right at the second switchback, elevation 1,900-1,920 ft. Parking is limited, there are no facilities, and the road is reportedly narrow enough that potholes are unavoidable. From the car, Mt Pugh Trail #644 climbs steadily through mature forest with a few stream crossings for about 1.5 miles to Lake Metan (Metam) at roughly 3,180-3,260 ft — this is the last reliable water on the route, so tank up here. The trail rounds the north side of the lake and then switchbacks hard up steep forested slopes, breaking out into an open boulder-strewn basin at around 4,900 ft before topping out at Stujack Pass, 5,700-5,750 ft, at about 4.5 miles. Above the pass the character changes completely: the path climbs leftward out of the notch on heather, contours the east side of the ridge, crosses the head of a small permanent snowfield and takes to the crest on chipped, blasted ledges. Continue past the class 3 rock step; the Pika Slab crag band is on the heather slopes immediately above the trail between that step and the summit, roughly 5 miles and 4,700 ft above the car.
descent: Downclimb class 3 to the right off the ledge, regain the trail, and reverse the Northwest Ridge scramble and Trail #644 to the car.
itinerary: Day trip. This is a single very long day: leave the trailhead at first light, reach Lake Metan in about 45-60 minutes, Stujack Pass in roughly 2.5-3 hours, and the Pika Slab crag band about 30-45 minutes above the pass. Climb the slab (a matter of minutes), continue to the summit for the view if weather allows, then reverse everything, allowing 2-3 hours down. Budget 7-9 hours car to car and be honest that the 5,300 ft of gain on the full peak day is among the largest of any Washington trail that reaches a true summit. If you want a shorter summit day there are a few camp spots at the base of Stujack Pass, but water above Lake Metan is unreliable, so you must carry it up.

waypoints.name: Mount Pugh Trailhead, FR 2095 second switchback
Stujack Pass — decision point, scramble begins, Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary

name: Custer-Rahm Traverse
approach: Reached from the summit of either Mount Rahm (via the Standard Route/Glacier or South Side) or Mount Custer (via its South Ridge), not from a trailhead directly.
descent: From Custer, descend via Custer's South Ridge; from Rahm, descend via the South Side route.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: This one is different. The approach starts in British Columbia — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

itinerary: Typically day 2 or 3 of a Depot Creek (Ouzel Lake) or Silver Creek approach trip: climb one peak via its standard line, make the traverse (about an hour), then descend the other peak's own route back to camp.

waypoints.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
Route reference point (Custer-Rahm ridge, near Mount Custer)

name: South Side
approach: Two camps are used: Silver Lake (6,763 ft, reached via a long Silver Creek bushwhack from Ross Lake) or Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft, reached via the Depot Creek approach from Chilliwack Lake Road, BC — the easier of the two to reach). From Ouzel Lake, climb northeast up an obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle, then traverse and ascend southwestward below the Custer-Rahm ridge to the roughly 7,400-ft upper terrace. From Silver Lake, climb above the lakeside cliffs to the northwest, or walk the north shore west until the cliffs end, then climb talus/slabs north to the same terrace.
descent: Descend the same gully system, or make a long high traverse over to Mount Custer via the Custer-Rahm Traverse.
itinerary: Day 1: hike in to Ouzel Lake (via Depot Creek, including a border crossing) or Silver Lake (via the Silver Creek bushwhack) and camp. Day 2: climb the South Side route to Rahm's summit (about 2 hrs from Silver Lake or 3-5 hrs from Ouzel Lake) and return to camp, or continue to Custer/Spickard. Day 3: hike out.

name: Edmunds Headwall
approach: From Mowich Lake, hike through Spray Park and up the lower Ptarmigan Ridge to camps near 9,600 ft between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers, then drop to the Edmunds Glacier and the base of the headwall.
descent: Descend a standard route, typically traversing to the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier after topping out at Liberty Cap.

bivy.name: Lower Ptarmigan Ridge camp
bivy.notes: Bivy ground on lower Ptarmigan Ridge above Spray Park, from which parties drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. Mowich Lake has had no road access since the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165 closed in 2025, so check access first.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites on rock and snow

itinerary: 3-4 days: approach from Mowich to a base camp, climb the headwall in a summit day to Liberty Cap, then descend a standard route.

waypoints.name: Liberty Cap (route tops out here, below/at the NW rim)

name: Fuhrer Thumb
approach: From Paradise take the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista, descend the Nisqually Moraine west to the Nisqually Glacier, cross glacier westward, ascend Wilson Gully/Wilson Bench/Wilson Chute on west side of glacier to Lower Castle camp, then continue northwest to Fuhrer Thumb couloir
descent: Not typically down-climbed; descend via the Kautz Glacier, Ingraham Glacier, or Disappointment Cleaver through Camp Muir instead.

bivy.name: Castle camps on Wapowety Cleaver
bivy.notes: Two camp areas on the ridge below Wapowety Cleaver at the edge of the Wilson Glacier. Lower Castle, about 9,250 ft, has a few closely spaced rock rings for small parties; Upper Castle, 9,400 to 9,500 ft, has large rock rings and is where most parties camp. Wind-exposed.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites behind old rock windbreaks

itinerary: Done in 1-2 days similar to the Finger, with an early start to climb the couloir cold.

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: Drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) to Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to a pullout near milepost 3, just past a creek flowing over a concrete weir (about 2,950 ft), well short of the road's end at Hannegan Campground. From the pullout, cross Ruth Creek (a log crossing has been used) and bushwhack roughly 45 minutes through slide alder and devil's club to the base of the Wall Street couloir.
descent: Descend the ascent route

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

itinerary: Single-push day: drive to the Ruth Creek Road pullout near milepost 3 (2,950 ft); cross Ruth Creek and bushwhack to the base of Wall Street (~45 min); climb the snow couloir to the Northwest Glacier (~5,000 ft); cross the glacier to the 6,500-ft saddle; scramble the southeast ridge to the 7,191-ft summit (about 5.6 hours car-to-summit for one party); descend the same line (about 2.8 hours back to the car).

waypoints.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

name: Silver Glacier
approach: Two camp options are used. Via Silver Creek: arrange a Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reservation required) roughly 25 miles up Ross Lake to a drop-off at the Silver Creek mouth (1,600 ft); a trail climbs the north side of Silver Creek about 2.5 miles to an old cabin at 2,900 ft, after which the route continues cross-country (occasional blazes) across slide-alder and forest slopes to the Silver Lake basin camp (6,763 ft). Via Ouzel Lake: use the Depot Creek approach (see the Southwest Ridge route) to Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft), then climb toward and over the Custer-Spickard saddle. From Ouzel Lake, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle and step onto the Silver Glacier beyond it. From Silver Lake there is no saddle to cross: walk round the north side of the lake to its south-west end, then south across moraine and snow, skirting a small buttress, to the glacier toe at about 7,400 ft.
descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the summit step to the notch, then descend the glacier and gully back to the saddle and camp.
itinerary: Day 1: water-taxi and hike (or Depot Creek hike) in to camp at Silver Lake or Ouzel Lake. Day 2: from Ouzel Lake climb the gully to the Custer-Spickard saddle (from Silver Lake, cross the moraine to the glacier toe), cross the Silver Glacier, and climb the summit step (roughly 3-4 hours summit-bound from Silver Lake camp), then return to camp. Day 3: hike/water-taxi out.

name: Kamikaze Trail (SW Ridge Scramble)
approach: Follow the Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead on SE Mount Si Road to the signed Teneriffe Falls junction at about 0.9 mile, turn right, and follow the Teneriffe Falls Trail to the falls viewpoint at about 2.8 miles. From just below the viewpoint, the unofficial but well-traveled Kamikaze Trail boot track climbs directly up the forested southwest ridge/flank of the mountain, gaining about 2,300 ft in roughly one mile of steep, rocky, single-track tread before reaching the Kamikaze Ridge crest (~3,900 ft) and continuing to a cedar-grove shelf (~4,200 ft) that meets the upper mountain near the summit. The trailhead gate was reported locked at about 8 pm and unlocked around 7 am in May and August, so plan a loop that finishes before then.
descent: Downclimb the Kamikaze boot track the way you came, or descend via the standard Mount Teneriffe Trail through Rachor Pass for a ~10-mile loop.

bivy.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
bivy.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.
bivy.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
bivy.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
bivy.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

itinerary: Typical day trip: start early morning; ~1-1.5 hrs to the Teneriffe Falls/Kamikaze junction (2.8 mi); ~2-2.5 hrs of steep boot-track climbing to the ridge crest and summit (~4.1 mi, about +4,000 ft); short summit break; descend either back down Kamikaze (~2.5 hrs) or via the standard trail loop (~3-3.5 hrs).

name: Mount Teneriffe Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From I-90 take Exit 31 into North Bend and continue on North Bend Way; turn left (north) on SE Mount Si Road. Continue about 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, to the paved, ~70-car Mount Teneriffe Trailhead lot (Discover Pass required). From the lot, a half-mile access path switchbacks up through second-growth forest to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for about 1.5 miles through young forest and meadow, passing the signed spur to Teneriffe Falls at about 0.9 mile. Beyond the road grade the trail narrows and climbs via switchbacks (with a Middle Fork Snoqualmie viewpoint) for another ~2.7 miles, then continues about 2.3 more miles, dipping briefly to Rachor Pass (~4,200 ft saddle) before the final short, rocky summit scramble. The trailhead gate was reported locked at about 8 pm and unlocked around 7 am in May and August, so budget the descent to beat it.
descent: Retrace the standard trail back to the trailhead (13 mi round trip); alternatively descend via the Kamikaze Trail for a ~10-mile loop.

bivy.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
bivy.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.
bivy.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
bivy.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
bivy.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

itinerary: Typical day trip: start early morning; ~1.5-2 hrs for the first 2.8 mi; ~2.5-3 hrs more via the upper switchbacks and Rachor Pass to the summit (6.5 mi, +3,800 ft); 30-45 min on the summit; ~3 hrs back down the same trail. Budget 7-9 hours car-to-car.

name: Stoddard Buttress
approach: Same as the North Buttress: from the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the old roadbed trail and a climbers' path to Terror Creek at about 2,000 ft, cross it, and climb the very steep path up the Barrier, the ridge beyond. Follow its crest north into Stump Hollow, make a rising traverse to the 6,400 ft saddle northeast of The Chopping Block, and downclimb about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin to the high camp (~6,000 ft gain, ~7-7.5 hrs), then on the climbing day cross the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descend the Mustard Glacier to the base of the north face (2-3 hrs from camp). Stoddard's original approach used a two-day approach via Stettattle Ridge and the upper McMillan Creek cirque.
descent: Descend via established descent route, using rappels and downclimbing as necessary. Multiple anchor points required.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

itinerary: Day 1: hike to the high camp in Crescent Creek Basin. Day 2: alpine start, cross the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and Mustard Glacier to the route base, climb the buttress crest and knife-edge finish to the summit, descend via the West Ridge notch and gully rappels (a long day, ~17 hrs camp-to-camp for one party). Day 3: hike out.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

name: West Ridge
approach: From Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed ~4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track (pink flagging, moss-covered cliffs) to reach Crescent Creek Basin; total approach elevation gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit tower, then descend the notch pitch on existing sling anchors and down the gully, rappelling its steeper steps

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The working camp for Terror, in the basin under the peak. Published camps sit between roughly 6,000 and 6,200 ft — there is talk among parties of a named 'Crescent Camp' that several have gone looking for and not found, so treat this as a zone of flat spots rather than a fixed site. Getting here from Terror Basin means crossing the upper Barrier or the roughly 6,400 ft saddle by the Chopping Block and downclimbing a couple of hundred feet of loose class 3 into the basin, which is a real piece of ground in fog. Rodents have been reported working the rocks at dusk, so hang or armour your food. Times from this camp are long: parties report about seven hours up and four and a half back on Terror.
bivy.water: Streams coming off the slabs above the basin — one party found two of them beside their site; snowmelt-fed, so check rather than assume late in a dry season
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Crescent Creek cross-country zone, capped at six parties a night and six people per party. Camp on rock, snow or bare ground only, and keep 100 ft from the streams
bivy.capacity: Small flat pockets rather than one site; parties report hunting among rock and heather outcrops before settling, and one describes checking six or eight before finding a bench that was only marginally good enough

bivy.name: Chopping Block saddle camp
bivy.notes: The saddle on the Chopping Block ridge overlooking Crescent Creek Basin, and the camp parties rate most highly on this side of the range — an open grandstand on the Southern Pickets. It is a dry, exposed perch, so the trade is view and position against carrying your water. Being on the crest it also puts you above the basin, which means a downclimb of a couple of hundred feet to get onto the climbing terrain each morning.
bivy.water: None at the saddle itself. The nearest reported source on the way in is a small stream around 5,700 ft on the granite slabs below, so carry water up
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required; the Crescent Creek cross-country zone is capped at six parties a night and six people per party
bivy.capacity: Small; reports describe a single good spot on the saddle rather than a cluster of sites

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual first night for parties heading to Terror, about 400 ft below the 6,200 ft saddle at the top of the Goodell Creek boot path. It is not the camp you climb Terror from — from here you still have to traverse and cross the roughly 6,400 ft saddle by the Chopping Block and drop into Crescent Creek Basin — but it is the natural place to stop after 6,000 ft of gain, and parties who lose the light on the approach routinely take it as-is.
bivy.water: Silty streams running through the basin from the snowfields above; reliable in a normal season, filter and treat
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone; walk-up only, not reservable
bivy.capacity: Several sites on gravel and rock plus a two-person bivy platform; the zone allows six parties a night, six people per party

itinerary: Day 1: approach to Crescent Creek Basin (~6,000 ft gain). Day 2: climb the gully to the West Ridge notch, complete the short technical section and summit scramble, then descend the same way. Day 3: hike out.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east to the Thornton Lakes Road spur (near milepost 117, just west of Newhalem) and follow the rough, unpaved, high-clearance road about 5 miles to the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft). Hike the Thornton Lakes Trail — an old logging-road grade for the first ~2 miles, then steeper trail up to the ridge/pass (~4,900 ft) above the lakes — then descend to the lake outlet (~4,400-4,486 ft). Traverse the brushy, sometimes-faint climbers' path around the east/south side of middle Thornton Lake, then climb a long, loose scree/talus gully (roughly 1,200 ft of gain) to a col around 5,750-5,840 ft that serves as the standard bivy site.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and rappel the ridge crest back to the col, then descend the approach gully and trail to the trailhead.

bivy.name: The Triumph col
bivy.notes: The standard high camp, on the col northwest of the middle lake, gained by about 1,200 ft of steep talus and grass above the lakes — roughly seven and a half miles and 4,200 ft from the car. Flat ground, running water and a view straight into the Pickets. Published elevations disagree by about 150 ft, from roughly 5,750 to 5,900 ft, so do not plan an altitude-sensitive turnaround off a single figure. A rockier perch just below the col is also used and is well liked.
bivy.water: Snowmelt — a small stream running off the snowpack, and pools near the sites; parties who want more drop toward the stream at the foot of the nearby snowfield. Every published description is of meltwater, and none says when it fails, so treat it as unreliable once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, in the Triumph cross-country zone: maximum party of six, and only two permits issued per night, which makes it one of the harder zones to get. It is one of the few zones that can be reserved in advance; roughly 40% of capacity is held back for walk-ups issued the day before or the day of, from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount. Cross-country camping is allowed only on durable ground — snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.capacity: Several good bivy spots on and just north of the col — nobody has had to drop to the glacier for want of ground. The real limit is the permit: the Triumph zone takes two parties a night, six people each.

bivy.name: Thornton Lakes camp
bivy.notes: Where the maintained trail ends, about five and a half miles in, at the outlet of the lower lake. It is the easy, legal, reliable option and the one to take if you arrive late or the col is booked out — but it leaves a very long summit day, since the col is still a thousand-plus feet of steep talus and grass above you. Most parties climbing the ridge push past it.
bivy.water: The outlet of the lower lake, immediately at the sites.
bivy.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required. This is a designated camp rather than the Triumph cross-country zone, so it is a different reservation from the col — book the one you actually intend to sleep in.
